solutions.check: 30 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Bollocks stink with infection

parts.note: to hum is British slang for to smell bad
a bug is a minor infection

explanation.surface: Someone dismisses a bad smell as nonsense, or it is something smelly and infected.
explanation.walkthrough: Bollocks is British slang for nonsense, used here as an exclamation.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are dismissive exclamations meaning rubbish or nonsense, a synonym pairing.

clue.text: Tell all and dispose of the knockers

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to confide or confess everything
second meaning, read jokily: un- (remove) plus a word for breasts, knockers being slang for them

explanation.walkthrough: The second half is a comic literal reading of the word, splitting it into a prefix of removal and a word for the chest.
explanation.definitionFit: To unburden oneself by revealing secrets or feelings is the standard meaning of the verb.

clue.text: Cover behind with barium to get an award

indicators.note: to cover something is to wrap around it, so one piece goes on the outside of the other

parts.note: Ba is the chemical symbol for barium
aft means at the back, as on a ship

explanation.surface: Someone protecting their backside with a barium layer in order to win a prize.
explanation.walkthrough: The two letters of the symbol go round the word for behind, one on each side.
explanation.definitionFit: The British Academy Film and Television Arts gives its annual awards, themselves called by this acronym.

clue.text: Gordon's main debasement: not looking too happy

indicators.note: the main part here is the head of the name, so only its opening letter is kept

parts.note: the first letter of the name
lowering something degrades or debases it

explanation.surface: Gordon Brown's chief humiliation leaves him looking glum.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface evokes former PM Gordon Brown, famous for his scowl.
explanation.definitionFit: Glowering means scowling or staring angrily, which is a far from cheerful expression.

clue.text: Ruthlessness of, er, ruined bankers etc.

indicators.note: something ruined is wrecked out of its original form, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
the City is London's financial district, home of bankers and their like

explanation.surface: A hesitant remark about the ruthlessness of ruined bankers and their kind.
explanation.walkthrough: The City (of London) stands for the financial world as a whole.
explanation.definitionFit: Ferocity is savage fierceness, a near synonym of ruthless cruelty.

clue.text: Any fatso getting end away affected vision

indicators.note: affected suggests something altered or put on, so the letters are reordered
having its end sent away means the final letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, before losing its last letter

explanation.surface: Any fat man who gets his end away (has sex) is living in a dream.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting one's end away' is British slang for having sex, but here it trims the last letter of fatso.
explanation.definitionFit: A fantasy is an imagined vision of something desired, a synonym sense.

clue.text: Prince tipped over pint, having a hard on

indicators.note: a glass tipped over is upended, so in a down clue the word reads from bottom to top

parts.note: a jar is British slang for a pint of beer
taken as written
H is the pencil-grading abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: A royal knocks over his drink while sexually aroused.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' just places the last pieces after the overturned drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A rajah is an Indian king or prince, so the title is a fair equivalent.

clue.text: Princely description of a despised erection

definitions.text: Princely description of a despised erection

parts.words: Princely description of a despised erection
parts.note: surface reading: a royal's crude remark about something sexual
setter's reading: Prince Charles famously called a planned extension to the National Gallery a 'monstrous' boil-like growth on the face of a friend

explanation.walkthrough: In 1984 Prince Charles condemned a proposed National Gallery extension with this word, and it became the stock term for an ugly modern building.
explanation.definitionFit: The word for a boil or abscess became, through the Prince's speech, slang for a hated new building.

clue.text: Gross flatterers' tools?

parts.note: surface reading: the instruments of sycophants who overdo it
setter's reading: to flatter grossly is to 'lay it on with' a gardener's or plasterer's hand blade

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'lay it on with a trowel' means to flatter excessively, so the tool belongs to the gross flatterer.
explanation.definitionFit: Trowels are small hand tools for spreading plaster or digging, and the idiom ties them to heavy flattery.

clue.text: Brown "nothing working" the clown

parts.note: buff is a yellowish-brown colour
O looks like zero, nothing
a machine that is on is working

explanation.surface: Gordon Brown branded a clown, with nothing working for him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brown' looks like Gordon Brown, but it is a colour.
explanation.definitionFit: A buffoon is a joker or fool, a synonym for a clown.

clue.text: Politician-speak from Jack — a gas!

parts.note: J is the abbreviation for jack in a pack of cards
argon is a noble gas

explanation.surface: Someone called Jack finds political waffle hilarious, a gas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A gas' reads as slang for great fun, but it means a chemical element.
explanation.definitionFit: Jargon is specialised, often obscure language of a trade, such as the empty phrases politicians use.

clue.text: (& 12ac.) So, not secure at all, in the case of many bank loans?

definitions.text: So, not secure at all, in the case of many bank loans?

parts.note: surface reading: describing something risky

parts.words: in the case of many bank loans
parts.note: setter's reading: an idiom meaning completely secure, here ironic because mortgages on property proved anything but secure in the banking crash

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom normally means perfectly safe; the clue twists it after the 2008 crash, when loans secured on property went bad.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means utterly secure, and the question mark flags the irony that property-backed loans were not.

clue.text: see 11ac.
How a Mitford sister declared herself "entered by a short chap in French Resistance"

indicators.note: being entered by something means taking it inside, so a piece goes into the middle of the phrase

parts.words: How a Mitford sister declared herself
parts.note: Unity Mitford, one of the Mitford sisters, introducing herself
M. is the short form of Monsieur, a French man

explanation.surface: A Mitford sister announces herself as having been penetrated by a little Frenchman in the Resistance.
explanation.walkthrough: The Mitfords were famous English aristocratic sisters; Unity was one. 'French Resistance' looks like one phrase, but French belongs to the chap.
explanation.definitionFit: Immunity is resistance to infection or to legal action, a synonym in either sense.

clue.text: What's lower than swearing? Being obliged to tell the truth!

definitions.meaning: first meaning, read literally: beneath a sworn promise

definitions.text: Being obliged to tell the truth
definitions.meaning: second meaning: bound by a sworn promise in court

explanation.walkthrough: Swearing looks like bad language, but it is the oath sworn by a witness.
explanation.definitionFit: A witness bound by a sworn promise must tell the truth, which is the legal state the phrase names.

clue.text: He's biased, Bill, having been stuck in stir wrongly

definitions.note: a clause describing the person; the answer is the noun for him

indicators.note: being stuck in something means placed inside it
done wrongly means not in the right order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, before being rearranged
AC, short for account, is a bill

explanation.surface: A bigot named Bill has been wrongly locked up in prison.
explanation.walkthrough: Stir is slang for prison and Bill looks like a name, but stir supplies letters and Bill is an account.
explanation.definitionFit: A racist is a person prejudiced against other races, so he is biased.

clue.text: Port causes arse blockage

parts.note: an arse is a contemptible person, as is a rotter
a dam blocks a river

explanation.surface: Drinking port leads to constipation.
explanation.walkthrough: Port looks like the drink, but it is a harbour city; arse is British slang for a fool or cad.
explanation.definitionFit: Rotterdam in the Netherlands is one of Europe's largest seaports, an example of a port.

clue.text: Pet the area between waist and knees, follow?

parts.words: the area between waist and knees
parts.note: the lap is the top of the thighs when seated
to dog someone is to follow them

explanation.surface: An invitation to fondle someone's lap, then follow them.
explanation.walkthrough: Pet reads as a verb of fondling, but it is the noun for an animal.
explanation.definitionFit: A lapdog is a small dog kept as a pet, an example of the category.

clue.text: Stuck up sports body wants half of TV partnership — one for the City

indicators.note: stuck up means placed upward, so in a down clue the letters are read from the bottom

parts.note: the LTA is the Lawn Tennis Association, governing British tennis
Ant of Ant and Dec, a British TV presenting duo
a means one

explanation.surface: A snooty sporting body wants a TV presenter for London's financial district.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The City' looks like London's financial district; here City alone is the definition. Ant and Dec are a hugely popular British TV double act.
explanation.definitionFit: Atlanta, capital of Georgia, is an American city.

clue.text: Attack familiar old PM over what the West Midlands Police did?

definitions.text: what the West Midlands Police did

parts.note: a fit is a sudden attack, as of coughing
Ted Heath, British prime minister 1970-74, known familiarly as Ted
time that is up is over

explanation.surface: Asking whether the police were the ones who attacked a former prime minister.
explanation.walkthrough: The West Midlands Serious Crime Squad was disbanded in 1989 over fabricated evidence, notably in the Birmingham Six case.
explanation.definitionFit: To be fitted up is British slang for being framed with false evidence, which that police squad notoriously did.

clue.text: Maybe those getting obscenely large bonuses, fast squandered, act uneasy inside

definitions.text: Maybe those getting obscenely large bonuses

indicators.note: inside places the second jumbled word within the first
squandered money is scattered carelessly, so these letters are scattered into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, before rearranging

indicators.note: uneasy means unsettled, so the second set of letters is also jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, before rearranging

explanation.surface: Bankers on huge bonuses who spent fast now behave nervously.
explanation.definitionFit: Fat cats are wealthy, overpaid executives; 'maybe' marks bonus-takers as an example of them.

clue.text: Pressing need of old city gent (25% down) — call Treasury's no. 2 out

indicators.note: losing a quarter of a four-letter word means one letter is cut off
out means removed, so a letter is taken away from the word for call

parts.note: Ur is the ancient Mesopotamian city, a crossword favourite
taken as written, before losing its last letter
to cry is to call out

indicators.note: number two picks out the second letter of the word it follows

parts.note: the second letter of the word

explanation.surface: An old City gentleman, his pay cut by a quarter, urgently needs to phone the Treasury's deputy.
explanation.walkthrough: The R removed from the word for call is the letter selected, not something added.
explanation.definitionFit: Urgency is a pressing need or importance demanding immediate action, a synonym.

clue.text: Like many a Daily Mail headline in the manner of Mrs T. raving about "independence"

definitions.text: Like many a Daily Mail headline

parts.note: à la is French for in the manner of

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the jumbled letters go around the next piece
raving means wild and deranged, so these letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written, before rearranging
I is the abbreviation for independent

explanation.surface: Mail headlines resemble Margaret Thatcher ranting about independence.
explanation.walkthrough: Mrs T. is Margaret Thatcher; the Daily Mail is a British tabloid known for scare headlines.
explanation.definitionFit: Alarmist means exaggerating danger to cause fear, typical of scare-mongering tabloid headlines.

clue.text: To enter more firmly is an attribute of group relations

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to go over pencil with pen, making an entry permanent

definitions.text: is an attribute of group relations
definitions.meaning: second meaning, read as two words: something within one's family

explanation.walkthrough: Split differently, the letters say 'in kin', inside the family group, which is the second definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Inking in a pencilled entry confirms it, and 'in kin' describes something found within one's relatives.

clue.text: Guy likely to engender a burning desire in zealots?

parts.words: likely to engender a burning desire in zealots
parts.note: surface reading: something inspiring passionate longing in fanatics
setter's reading: the Guy Fawkes dummy burned on Bonfire Night, or any figure of a hated person zealots burn

explanation.walkthrough: On 5 November British people burn a dummy of Guy Fawkes, and protesters 'burn someone in effigy'; the burning desire is literal.
explanation.definitionFit: A guy is a stuffed dummy representing Guy Fawkes, a model figure of a person.

clue.text: Low-life Murdoch showing a bit of leg

indicators.note: showing means putting on display letters already present in the words before it

parts.note: found across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Rupert Murdoch, a low-life, flashing a bit of leg.
explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye regularly lampoons the media mogul Rupert Murdoch.
explanation.definitionFit: The femur is the thigh bone, a part of the leg.

clue.text: Almost cut off one's balls before leaders of South Kensington show up

indicators.note: almost means not quite complete, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: to unman is to castrate

indicators.note: leaders are the front-runners, so only initial letters are kept

parts.note: the first letters of the two words

explanation.surface: Nearly castrating oneself before the bigwigs of a posh London district turn up.
explanation.walkthrough: South Kensington is a wealthy area of west London.
explanation.definitionFit: To unmask someone is to expose or show them up for what they are.

clue.text: Belly, etc. wobbled, bad sign

indicators.note: something that has wobbled has been shaken about, so the letters move

parts.note: taken as written, before rearranging
an omen is a portent or sign

explanation.surface: A wobbling belly is a bad sign.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Etc.' widens belly to the whole region containing the stomach and bowels.
explanation.definitionFit: The abdomen is the belly and the organs within it, so 'etc.' covers the extra contents.

clue.text: Administered by whips a great deal

definitions.meaning: first meaning: strokes given with a whip
second meaning: British informal for plenty

explanation.walkthrough: Whips could be party whips enforcing discipline in Parliament, but here they are literal floggings.
explanation.definitionFit: Lashings are blows with a whip, and in British slang lashings of something means an abundance of it.

clue.text: Political commentator hugs disheartened supporter of Cameron — he suffers

indicators.note: to hug is to wrap around, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: Andrew Marr, the BBC political journalist

indicators.note: losing its heart means the middle letters of the word are removed

parts.note: David Cameron led the Conservatives, whose supporters are Tories

explanation.surface: A TV pundit embraces a dejected Conservative supporter of David Cameron.
explanation.definitionFit: A martyr is a person who suffers or dies for a cause.
